How I would start this off is\:In today's video we're going to cover how your retirement plan is going to be built out and the three different layers that go into how the app works and how your retirement plan is going to work.

1. The first layer is going to be your baseline. This includes all of the data and information that I just covered: all the data and information that is true for your life right now. This is what your current income is, what your current spending is, all of your current assets, debts, every aspect about your financial life that is true today. Then after we have all of the data that's true today, we're also going to have another aspect of your baseline and foundation of your plan, which is going to be the assumptions that we're making today about the future. These are things like what you feel like is a conservative baseline to use for future asset performance and things like inflation, what your future income is going to grow at.
2. The second layer is going to be future life events. These are things that you genuinely expect to happen in the future and that you can reasonably predict as future expenses. They might not be happening now but you have a high level of confidence that they're happening in the future. Some examples of these things are:

- future college payments
- what your spending is going to be in retirement and how that might change
- a new car that you're planning on purchasing
- a house that you're planning on purchasing or selling
- or future long-term care expenses later in retirement

Adding these things in your plan will correctly calculate the amount of money that you need and just gives us a more accurate projection of what your realistic retirement date is 
Then the third layer is going to be scenarios. I think it's extremely important to really think through the assumptions that we're making about what the future looks like. Every projection and number in your plan is going to be built on top of these numbers so getting them right or as close to honest is going to matter more than any other single decision that you're going to make. There are six main categories I would put assumptions into. These are things like:

- your investment returns, including Bitcoin
- inflation
- what you're spending is now and where spending is going to be in retirement
- what your life expectancy is
- what your savings rate is going to be
- any future life events that change where your income or your spending is going to be

I think one of the most important things to think through is that it's a good thing to lean conservative when it comes to things like Bitcoin and other assets and what their returns are going to be. If we make assumptions that are too optimistic, it's going to make you feel good about where you're at and what your plan is today. The problem is that if they're wrong, you're not going to find out till years down the road. Being conservative means that you might be surprised to the upside and give yourself the ability to spend more in a worst-case scenario if you're wrong. Being optimistic means that if you're wrong, there are more severe consequences, like having to work longer than you thought you might have or you won't have the ability to spend what you really want to in retirement

This is a quick example. Let's say we have someone that's 45 years old. They're holding 1.75 Bitcoin and spending around $80,000 a year. If we were to set Bitcoin's returns at just a flat CAGR of 40% forever, this is gonna land their earliest retirement age at around 50, for example. If we were to run Bitcoin at a 20% declining rate as adoption grows, this matches more accurately with reality and what we've seen in the past about Bitcoin's price performance and how declines or returns have been declining as the asset class grows. In this scenario the retirement date is gonna move from 50 years old to 58 years old. This is a difference of eight years in this example just from one input changing as far as when it comes to Bitcoin's price. This is why it's really important to think through what you personally feel like is a conservative and realistic number about what Bitcoin can do in the future. So when it comes to the app, the four major default settings are going to be:

- a conservative model
- a moderate model
- an aggressive model
- the Power Law

The conservative is going to start around 20% return per year and it's going to decline to around 6% over time. The moderate starts at around 30% and aggressive is going to start around 40% and it declines more slowly over time. The last one's going to be the Power Law. If you don't know much about the Power Law, this is a declining return profile that uses a price curve that's fitted to Bitcoin's entire price history going back to 2009. It just maps every day's prices and then draws a curve into the future about what we can predict about where Bitcoin's going to go based off of a growing asset class in Bitcoin's network effect. As the asset class grows it's reasonable to predict that the returns will decline going forward. All the presets in the app decline over time and the reason is that as Bitcoin gets larger it gets harder to move as an asset class. When Bitcoin was $10 billion for the entire asset, one big news event or institution could move the entire market. Now that Bitcoin's a trillion dollars, doubling the asset class takes trillions of new dollars coming in. At $10 trillion it takes tens of trillions of dollars. The declining growth curve is just more honest and realistic about how I see Bitcoin's growth playing out in the future. If you do want to create your own returns going into the future, in the assumptions tab in the app, there's an option for you to create custom return windows. You can put in different assumptions about Bitcoin's future or any other asset's future if you feel like that's a better assumption about what you want to implement for your plan.
